ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Amelia Earhart Synthetic CCD

text.paragraph: New patient, a private pilot, with five months of nasal blockage, discolored drainage, facial pressure and reduced smell: history, anterior rhinoscopy, symptom scoring, saline irrigation and an intranasal steroid, and fitness to fly. Concerns: Her nose is always blocked, her face aches over the left cheek and forehead, and she has lost much of her sense of smell; Pressure pain on descent has made her cancel flights, and she wants to know when it is safe to fly and which medicines she may take as a pilot; She had sinus operations after a bad infection years ago and wants to avoid another operation unless it will really help. [S]

Fluticasone propionate 50 mcg per spray nasal spray, two sprays in each nostril once daily, aimed away from the septum

list.item: Nasal blockage, thick discolored nasal drainage, pressure over the left cheek and forehead, and a reduced sense of smell for about five months, with pressure pain in the left cheek on descent when flying. Anterior rhinoscopy shows swollen, red inferior turbinates without visible polyps or pus; SNOT-22 52. Suspected chronic rhinosinusitis; nasal endoscopy and otolaryngology consultation booked: resolved, confirmed [S]

Synthetic modern episode linked to her documented chronic sinus trouble: active, confirmed [S]

tr.td: New patient, a private pilot, with five months of nasal blockage, discolored drainage, facial pressure and reduced smell: history, anterior rhinoscopy, symptom scoring, saline irrigation and an intranasal steroid, and fitness to fly
Nasal endoscopy and otolaryngology consultation: diagnosis, an acute exacerbation, and the plan for imaging and surgery
Same-day sick visit for left ear pain after a flight
Review after ten weeks of medical therapy: symptom score, sinus CT result, and the decision about surgery
Review five weeks after endoscopic sinus surgery: symptoms, healing, pathology, and return to flying

code.displayName: Periodic reevaluation and management of healthy individual

tr.td: First-line medical therapy: high-volume saline irrigation twice daily and fluticasone nasal spray two sprays in each nostril daily, with technique taught in clinic; topical decongestant sprays stopped because rebound blockage follows use beyond a few days
Otolaryngology consultation with nasal endoscopy to confirm the diagnosis with objective evidence and to look for nasal polyps, and advice on further treatment, imaging, and surgery

Check for conditions that change management (asthma, cystic fibrosis, immune deficiency, ciliary dyskinesia, aspirin sensitivity, a dental source): history, blood eosinophils and total IgE; no imaging and no antifungal treatment at this stage

Fitness to fly: no flying while blocked or in pain, as 14 CFR 61.53 requires; a 48-hour ground trial before flying on any new medicine; only medicines the FAA accepts for pilots (nasal steroid sprays, saline, non-sedating antihistamines, pseudoephedrine); the diphenhydramine night tablet stopped, with at least 60 hours before flying after any dose; and practice of ear and sinus clearing on descent

Culture-directed antibiotic for the acute exacerbation with pus in the middle meatus: an endoscopically guided culture and amoxicillin-clavulanate for 10 days; no oral corticosteroid, because her disease has no polyps; no long-term antibiotic

CT of the sinuses after at least eight weeks of irrigation and nasal steroid plus the antibiotic course, with the SNOT-22 repeated, to decide whether endoscopic sinus surgery is appropriate and to plan it

Endoscopic sinus surgery on the left (maxillary antrostomy, anterior ethmoidectomy, and frontal recess dissection), chosen by her after a shared decision because the SNOT-22 stayed above 20 with disease on CT after appropriate medical therapy; then budesonide added to the saline rinse, cleaning of the sinuses in the ear, nose and throat clinic, and no flying until the surgeon clears her
SNOT-22 total score below 20 by four months
Fly without sinus or ear pressure pain, and only when she meets the FAA rule of not flying while symptomatic, by four months
Flying again since the ear, nose and throat clearance three weeks after surgery, without pressure pain
Use only medicines acceptable for pilots, with a 48-hour ground trial of each new medicine and no sedating antihistamine
No-go medicines stopped at intake; each new medicine started on a non-flying day
Saline irrigation and the nasal steroid used daily with correct technique
Daily use with correct technique at ten weeks; no nosebleeds
